title: The birth of rock'n'roll
subject: art
description: In the mid-1950s, Black blues and white country merge: Elvis, Chuck Berry and Little Richard invent rock'n'roll.

hero.hook: One scream, one electric guitar, and teenage America had its music.

blocks.text: Rock'n'roll did not come out of nowhere in the mid-**1950s**. In the United States, it fused musical traditions long kept apart by racial barriers: blues, country and [[gospel]].
Three figures carried the break: **Elvis Presley**, **Chuck Berry** and **Little Richard**. More than a style, it was a youth culture, and a mirror of the tensions of [[segregation]].

sections.title: Blues, country and rhythm and blues

blocks.text: Until then, two worlds lived side by side in the South: Black culture (electric blues, gospel) and white culture (country). The bridge was called [[rhythm and blues]], an urban, electrified version of the blues that from the late 1940s on won over white teenagers hungry for rhythm.

**Rockabilly** appeared, a hybrid of country and blues. **Elvis Presley**, from Tupelo, grew up between Pentecostal churches and the blues of Beale Street. In **1954**, at the Memphis studio of the producer [[Sam Phillips]], he recorded *That's All Right*. But [[Segregation in the American music industry]] was still the rule: Black artists were often confined to marginal circuits, while a white singer could cross into the national market.
The term “rock'n'roll” first described the rolling of a ship, then, in the blues of the 1920s, the sexual act, before the DJ [[Alan Freed]] made it famous.
At [[Sun Records]], Elvis became the icon. His body in motion shocked puritan America and sealed the alliance between rock and adolescence.

blocks.caption: Elvis at Sun Records: rock finds its face

blocks.text: **Chuck Berry** brought the structure: the guitar **riff**, a repeated figure that became the backbone of the song. He sang about cars, high school and freedom. **Little Richard** screamed and pounded the piano standing up, raw energy inherited from the fervor of gospel.

blocks.caption: Chuck Berry: the guitar riff as the grammar of rock
Little Richard: the scream and the piano as an explosion

blocks.text: In 1956, on *The Ed Sullivan Show*, the cameras filmed Elvis only from the waist up. His hip movements were judged too scandalous.

For the first time, Black and white teenagers shared the same idols, despite the [[Jim Crow laws]]. But the integration stayed one-sided. The industry churned out [[covers]], watered-down white versions of Black hits that got better radio promotion. Pat Boone's *Tutti Frutti* long outsold Little Richard's original.
Despite this plunder, rock fed the spirit of the [[Civil Rights Movement]]. By breaking their parents' codes, the young people of the 1950s began a moral and racial reckoning for America.
Chuck Berry did not take a band on tour. He hired local musicians in each city, to save money and to avoid racial trouble at the hotel.

sections.title: From the British Invasion to the legacy

blocks.text: Around **1960**, the first wave ran out of steam: Elvis went into the army, Little Richard turned to religion. But the genre had already won over the United Kingdom. The **Beatles** and the **Rolling Stones** reworked the American standards, and the “British Invasion” turned rock into an art of albums and protest. Without the opening of **1954**, the counter-cultures of the 1960s would not have had the same engine of sound.

blocks.text: Born in 1954 from the fusion of rhythm and blues and country, the rock'n'roll of Elvis, Berry and Little Richard gave young people a first shared language against segregation.
